title: OKRs - Goals That Drive Action
subtitle: Your team sets goals at the start of the quarter that nobody looks at again. Or your goals are
useWhen: so vague that you can't tell at the end of the quarter whether you achieved them. Activity is high, progress is unclear.
howToUse: OKRs were developed by Andy Grove at Intel in the 1970s and popularised by John Doerr at Google. An Objective is a qualitative, inspiring statement of where you want to go. Key Results are 2–4 specific, measurable outcomes that prove you've arrived. The critical rule: Key Results measure outcomes, not activities. 'Launch the new feature' is a task. 'Achieve 40% feature adoption among active users within 60 days' is a Key Result. OKRs work because they separate what you want to achieve from how you'll know you've achieved it.
steps: Write the Objective as something that would genuinely excite the team, not a business metric.
Key Results must be measurable, if you can't put a number on it, it's not a Key Result.
Set 3–5 OKRs per quarter. More dilutes focus. Fewer creates over-dependence on one outcome.

Review OKRs in weekly team meetings, not just at quarter end. Set goals your team actually works toward, not ones they forget by week two Hitting 100% of your Key Results every quarter isn't success, it's a sign you set them too safe. OKRs work as a stretch tool, not a performance review. If your team is always green, you're measuring comfort, not progress. Ambitious Targets Aren't the Point
origin: Andy Grove, Intel — MBO adapted to OKRs · John Doerr, Google, 1999
promptBody:
Act as an OKR coach and strategist.
My business context    :  [COMPANY STAGE, TEAM SIZE, MAIN FOCUS]
This quarter's priority :  [THE ONE THING THAT MATTERS MOST]
Current challenges       :  [WHAT IS HOLDING GROWTH BACK]
Write 3 OKRs for this quarter:
For each OKR:
OBJECTIVE      :  Inspiring, qualitative direction (1 sentence)
KEY RESULT 1 :  Specific, measurable outcome with number
KEY RESULT 2 :  Specific, measurable outcome with number
KEY RESULT 3 :  Specific, measurable outcome with number
Then: flag any Key Result that is actually a task disguised as an outcome - and rewrite it.
Suggest a weekly check-in question for each OKR.

proTip:
The most common OKR failure is writing Key Results that measure activity instead of
outcome. 'Conduct 20 customer interviews' is activity. 'Identify 3 validated insights that
change our roadmap' is outcome. Your team can tick off activity without moving the
needle. Only outcomes tell you if you're actually winning.
